name: Nikhil Ito

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for sitting down with me, Nikhil. I'm a field researcher from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for any company, union, party or government. Everything's confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Can you start by walking me through a normal day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run blasthole drills at an iron ore mine, the big rigs that drill the holes the explosives go into. These days it's a mix: two days a week I'm in the cab of a drill on the bench, and the rest I'm in the operations centre in town, supervising three drills that run themselves while I watch the screens and step in when one gets confused. I'm the drill team lead, so I also plan the drill patterns with the engineers.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what's tiring?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love the problem-solving. When a drill hits a band of hard rock and the autonomy system just stops and sulks, I'm the one who figures out what it's seeing. I use AI tools every day, to check drill logs, to write the shift report, even to teach myself a bit of coding in the evenings. What's tiring is the screens, honestly, eight hours of four monitors gives me a headache I never had in the cab.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Hana teaches science at the high school, and we've got Ravi, who's eleven, and Mei, who's eight. We've got a mortgage on a place near the river, maybe twelve years left. We've got more than six months put away, plus some index funds I started buying when I was thirty, which I check far too often.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a bit of a let-down, honestly, and I'd say it online too, because I've been one of the people at work saying this stuff is the future. I'd own that I was too excited. I'd still say the tools are useful, just not magic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means my job stays exactly as it is, which is a pretty good job. Part of me would be relieved for the guys on my crew who are nervous. Part of me would be bored, because I like it when things move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much. I'd keep using the AI tools I already use, keep putting a few hundred a month into index funds, and probably push the company to finish the drill autonomy project properly, since it'd be just the normal kind of automation. I'd keep going with my evening coding, because it's fun.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Maybe a little deflated, like a football match that ends nil-nil.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said some of your crew are nervous now. Who are you thinking of?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pete, mainly. He's been drilling for twenty-five years and he won't touch the operations centre, he says screens give him the creeps. Every time a new autonomous drill comes in, he asks me quietly if he's next. In this picture I could tell him honestly: no, mate, you're fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the coding, what's it for if nothing changes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's partly a hobby, partly a hedge. I wrote a little program that reads our drill logs and flags holes that went off-angle, and the engineers actually use it now. Even if AI is just hype, knowing how to make the computer do the boring bits makes my day better.

S0.say: Nikhil would admit online and at work that he'd been too excited about AI and the tools turned out useful but not magic. He'd own being one of the loudest voices for it.
S0.think: Privately he sees his job staying as it is, which is a good outcome. He'd be relieved for nervous colleagues but a little bored, because he likes things moving.
S0.do: Keeps using his everyday AI tools and putting a few hundred a month into index funds. Pushes the company to finish the drill autonomy project and keeps coding in the evenings for fun and as a hedge.
S0.feel: Calm and slightly deflated, like a match that ends without a goal.
S0.quote: In this picture I could tell him honestly: no, mate, you're fine.
S0.fieldNote: Nikhil is unusual in being a little disappointed by the plateau. He already supervises self-driving drills and writes his own small programs, so the mild picture changes nothing for him. His thoughts went quickly to Pete, the veteran driller who is scared of screens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the version we can actually get right, if we share the gains. At work I'd push for the time saved to go into shorter weeks and training, not just fewer workers. I'd post that online too, I'm the kind of guy who posts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it's good for me. I already sit between the drill and the screen, and in steady change that middle seat becomes the most important one on site. I'd probably get promoted, which feels a bit awkward when I know some guys would be losing seats.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the company straight away to run a proper course for drillers moving into the operations centre, and offer to help teach it. I'd learn more on the data side, maybe a short online certificate in data analysis. And I'd be at the union meeting arguing for a four-day week, funded out of what the automation saves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and a bit excited, with some guilt mixed in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said guilt. Where does that come from?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: From Pete, again. I'd be getting a pay rise from the same change that's making him miserable. I'd try to drag him into the operations centre with me, but you can't make someone love screens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Hana say about all this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd tell me to slow down before I sign up for three courses at once. She sees the same thing at school, with kids using AI for homework, and she's more cautious than me. We balance each other out.

S1.say: Nikhil would say steady change is the version society can get right if the gains are shared. He'd push at work and online for the time saved to fund shorter weeks and training.
S1.think: Privately he sees it as good for him, since his seat between the drill and the screen becomes the most important one on site. He expects a promotion but feels awkward about benefiting while others lose seats.
S1.do: Asks the company to run a course for drillers moving into the operations centre and offers to help teach it. Takes a short online certificate in data analysis and argues at the union for a four-day week funded by automation savings.
S1.feel: Calm and a bit excited, with some guilt about colleagues who'd lose out.
S1.quote: I'd be getting a pay rise from the same change that's making him miserable.
S1.fieldNote: Nikhil is the person automation would promote, and he knows it. His progressive views show up as wanting the gains shared through shorter weeks and training. The guilt about Pete is genuine and recurring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this needs a public response on the scale of a war. Tax the companies that own the AI, fund an income for everyone, and do it now, not after the layoffs. I'd be posting about it every day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's the first picture that really bites me. If AI can do almost anything, then the operations centre runs itself too, and my special middle seat is just another seat. I'd be fine for money for a while, but I'd have no idea what my career is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First week, I'd move a chunk of our index funds into something steadier and pay a lump off the mortgage. I'd try to get into the company's AI team, the people setting the system up, because even AGI needs someone to install and check it for the first year or two. And I'd join or start a local campaign for an income guarantee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not panicked, because we've got savings and Hana's job, but there's a real tightness in my chest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd move money into something steadier. What exactly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably cash and government bonds, the boring stuff. I know the AI companies' shares would probably go up, and I've thought about buying some. But it feels wrong to bet on the thing that's putting my mates out of work, so I'd maybe put a little in and feel bad about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would two years of warning even give you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Barely anything, maybe six months to get onto that installation team. I'm used to being early, but two years means everybody's late, including me. The thing that bugs me is that being adaptable doesn't save you if the whole board gets wiped.

S2.say: Nikhil would call for a public response on the scale of a war, with companies that own AI taxed to fund an income for everyone. He'd post about it daily.
S2.think: Privately he sees it as the first picture that really bites him, because the operations centre would run itself and his middle seat would vanish. Money would hold for a while, but his career path would disappear.
S2.do: Moves part of the family's index funds into cash and bonds in the first week and pays a lump off the mortgage. Tries to join the company's AI installation team and joins or starts a local campaign for an income guarantee.
S2.feel: Anxious, with a tight chest, but held short of panic by savings and Hana's job.
S2.quote: Being adaptable doesn't save you if the whole board gets wiped.
S2.fieldNote: The two-year picture is where Nikhil's early-adopter advantage stops working, and he said so plainly. He's torn about buying shares in AI companies, wanting the hedge but feeling it betrays his crew. His progressive politics get louder as his own position weakens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to build something fair if we start the planning this year. I'd push for a transition fund, retraining for everyone, and public ownership of some of the AI systems. I'd say it at the union and online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is enough for me to land somewhere. I'd ride the operations centre for two or three years, then move into setting up and checking these systems at other mines. And I'd have time to think about what comes after.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the data certificate this year and aim for a role on the company's automation rollout within twelve months. I'd keep investing, maybe a bit more cautiously. I'd also talk with Hana about whether one of us should train for something human, like her moving into school counselling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. There's a plan, so it's not anxiety, but I keep thinking about what happens in year six.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you mean by year six?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Once AGI fully arrives, even the setup work runs itself. So the five years get me a good run and pay off the house, but then I'm still standing there in 2032 wondering what's next. I'd want to have the mortgage done by then so the question isn't scary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you explain the five-year picture to Ravi?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ravi's into robots, so he'd probably think it's cool. I'd tell him the robots are amazing but people still matter, and we have to make sure the robots work for everybody, not just the owners. He'd roll his eyes, but I'd say it anyway.

S3.say: Nikhil would say five years is enough to build a fair transition if planning starts this year. He'd push for a transition fund, universal retraining and public ownership of some AI systems.
S3.think: Privately he expects to land well, riding the operations centre for a few years before moving into installing and checking systems at other mines. He worries about what comes after once even that work is automated.
S3.do: Starts the data certificate this year and aims for a role on the company's automation rollout within twelve months. Keeps investing more cautiously and talks with Hana about her training for school counselling.
S3.feel: Uneasy, with a plan in hand but a nagging worry about what happens after the five years.
S3.quote: I'm still standing there in 2032 wondering what's next.
S3.fieldNote: With five years Nikhil plays to his strengths and moves early, but he sees past the transition to an empty year six. He's thinking about the household as a unit, considering which partner should move into human-centred work. Clearing the mortgage before the end point is his main safety goal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade gives us no excuse not to share this properly. I'd push for a shorter working week as the machines take over, and an income for everyone funded by the companies. Honestly, I'd say this could be the best thing that ever happened to working people if we fight for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years is plenty for me. I'd be fifty-three, mortgage gone, and I'd have had a good decade working on automation, which pays well. If the politics go right, I'd see it as freedom, not loss.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the data certificate, then a proper qualification in automation systems over three or four years, part-time. I'd keep investing steadily and pay off the mortgage by about year eight. I'd also get involved in politics locally, maybe the council, because the decisions made in those ten years matter more than anything I do at work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and a bit hopeful. The worry is about the politics, not my own situation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said if the politics go right. What if they don't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd be fine and lots of other people wouldn't, which would make me furious. People like Pete, who never wanted to touch a screen, would be left with nothing. That's why I'd be doing the council thing, I don't want to be comfortable in a town that's falling apart.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you be doing with your days at the end of it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Teaching, maybe, coaching Mei's soccer team, fixing up an old motorbike. If the machines do the work and the money's shared, I'd happily spend my fifties being useful in ways nobody pays for. That's the dream version, anyway.

S4.say: Nikhil would say a decade leaves no excuse for not sharing the gains, pushing for a shorter week and a company-funded income for everyone. He'd argue it could be the best thing for working people if they fight for it.
S4.think: Privately he thinks ten years is plenty for him, since he'd be 53 with the mortgage gone after a well-paid decade in automation. If the politics go right, he'd see it as freedom.
S4.do: Takes the data certificate and then a part-time qualification in automation systems over three or four years. Invests steadily, aims to clear the mortgage by year eight and gets involved in local council politics.
S4.feel: Calm and a bit hopeful, with his worry pointed at the politics rather than himself.
S4.quote: I don't want to be comfortable in a town that's falling apart.
S4.fieldNote: For Nikhil ten years is time to prosper, and he talks about the end point as possible freedom. His concern shifts to whether the gains are shared, with Pete as the face of who might be left behind. Of all his answers, this is where his politics and his own interest line up most neatly.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. It's the only one where being early doesn't help, because everyone's late. What would help is a guaranteed income paid for by the companies that own the AI, and a government that acts in months, not years.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Who owns the robots. Everyone asks if robots will take jobs, but the real question is who gets the money when they do. If the answer is a few companies, we're in trouble whatever the timeline.

headlineQuote: Everyone asks if robots will take jobs, but the real question is who gets the money when they do.
portrait: Nikhil Ito is a 43-year-old drill team lead at an iron ore mine who already splits his week between a drill cab and a town operations centre supervising self-driving rigs. He uses AI every day, codes in the evenings and invests in index funds, with a science teacher partner, two kids and a mortgage. In the milder pictures automation would promote him, which leaves him a little guilty about colleagues like Pete. The two-year AGI picture is the only one that truly rattles him, because adaptability can't help when everyone is late. Over ten years he sees possible freedom, as long as the gains are shared, and he'd go into local politics to make sure.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because being early gives no advantage when everyone is caught late.
whatWouldHelp: A guaranteed income funded by the companies that own the AI, and a government that acts within months rather than years.
